item.title: Choosing the best Investment Opportunities
item.description:
We are going to try to create a model that will identify the best stocks based on multiple KPIs. specifically we are going to concentrate on growth and stability.

  1. we need to download the following libraries.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import plotly.express as px
  1. upload your financial dataset

# Load dataset
file_path = r'C:\Users\julioa\OneDrive - Default Directory\Desktop\DeskTop\Data Science III\nyse-stocks.csv'
stocks_df = pd.read_csv(file_path)

# Clean column names
stocks_df.columns = stocks_df.columns.str.strip()
  1. Identifie the features you want to use for your predictions and clean the data. below is the code.

features = [
    'Market Cap', 'PE Ratio', 'Div. Yield', 'Change YTD', 'Return 1Y',
    'Rev. Growth (Q)', 'NetInc Growth (Q)', 'Gross Margin', 'Oper. Margin',
    'PEG Ratio','Rev. Growth', 'ROIC', 'EPS Growth', 'PT Upside (%)'
]
rating_column = 'Top Rating'
analyst_column = 'Top Analysts'

# 2) Clean 'Total Debt' and 'Total Cash' FIRST (before computing the ratio)
for col in ['Total Debt', 'Total Cash']:
    if col not in stocks_df.columns:
        raise KeyError(f"Column '{col}' not found in DataFrame.")
    s = stocks_df[col]
    # If it's object/string, strip $, % and commas, then convert to numeric
    if s.dtype == 'object':
        s = s.str.replace(r'[\$,%,]', '', regex=True)
    stocks_df[col] = pd.to_numeric(s, errors='coerce')

# 3) Compute Debt-to-Cash safely (avoid divide-by-zero -> NaN)
stocks_df['Debt-to-Cash'] = stocks_df['Total Debt'] / stocks_df['Total Cash'].replace({0: np.nan})
# Replace infinite values (if any) with NaN
stocks_df.replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan, inplace=True)

# 4) Add 'Debt-to-Cash' to features after it exists
features.append('Debt-to-Cash')

# 5) Select relevant columns
selected_df = stocks_df[['Symbol'] + features + [rating_column, analyst_column]].copy()

# 6) Robust cleaning & conversion for all feature columns (only use .str on object dtypes)
symbols_to_strip = r'[\$,%,]'
for col in features:
    if col not in selected_df.columns:
        raise KeyError(f"Column '{col}' not found after selection.")
    series = selected_df[col]
    if series.dtype == 'object':
        series = series.str.replace(symbols_to_strip, '', regex=True)
    selected_df[col] = pd.to_numeric(series, errors='coerce')

# 7) Convert Top Analysts to numeric
selected_df[analyst_column] = pd.to_numeric(selected_df[analyst_column], errors='coerce')

# 8) Impute missing numeric values with median
numeric_cols = selected_df[features + [analyst_column]]
selected_df[numeric_cols.columns] = numeric_cols.fillna(numeric_cols.median())

symbols_to_strip = r'[\$,%,]'
for col in features:
    if col not in selected_df.columns:
        raise KeyError(f"Column '{col}' not found in DataFrame.")
    s = selected_df[col]
    if s.dtype == 'object':
        s = s.str.replace(symbols_to_strip, '', regex=True)
    selected_df[col] = pd.to_numeric(s, errors='coerce')

# Convert Top Analysts to numeric
selected_df[analyst_column] = pd.to_numeric(selected_df[analyst_column], errors='coerce')

# Replace infinities and handle missing values
selected_df.replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan, inplace=True)
numeric_cols = selected_df[features + [analyst_column]]
selected_df[numeric_cols.columns] = numeric_cols.fillna(numeric_cols.median())
  1. if you have any categories that needs rating this is the time to do that.

rating_map = {
    'Strong Buy': 5,
    'Buy': 4,
    'Hold': 3,
    'Sell': 2,
    'Strong Sell': 1,
    '(blank)': 0
}
selected_df['Top Rating Score'] = selected_df[rating_column].map(rating_map).fillna(0)

all_features = features + ['Top Rating Score', analyst_column]
normalized_df = selected_df.copy()
for feature in all_features:
    normalized_df[feature] = (
        selected_df[feature] - selected_df[feature].min()
    ) / (selected_df[feature].max() - selected_df[feature].min())
  1. this is where we are going add some weights to each of the features. it will all depend where you want your prediction to lean. growth or stability.

weights = {
    'Market Cap': 0.07,
    'PE Ratio': 0.07,
    'Div. Yield': 0.05,
    'Change YTD': 0.07,
    'Return 1Y': 0.12,
    'Rev. Growth': 0.07,
    'Rev. Growth (Q)': 0.07,
    'NetInc Growth (Q)': 0.07,
    'Gross Margin': 0.07,
    'Oper. Margin': 0.07,
    'Top Rating Score': 0.15,
    'Top Analysts': 0.09,
    'PEG Ratio': 0.08,
    'Rev. Growth 3Y': 0.10,
    'ROIC': 0.08,
    'Debt-to-Cash': 0.05,
    'EPS Growth': 0.07,
    'PT Upside (%)': 0.08
}
  1. If you would like to add some bonuses to some of the features, this is the code that will help you do that.

normalized_df['Score'] = sum(normalized_df[f] * w for f, w in weights.items() if f in normalized_df.columns)

normalized_df['Bonus'] = 0
normalized_df.loc[selected_df['PEG Ratio'] < 1.5, 'Bonus'] += 0.02
normalized_df.loc[selected_df['Rev. Growth'] > 10, 'Bonus'] += 0.02
normalized_df.loc[selected_df['Gross Margin'] > 40, 'Bonus'] += 0.02
normalized_df.loc[selected_df['ROIC'] > 10, 'Bonus'] += 0.02
normalized_df.loc[selected_df['Debt-to-Cash'] < 1, 'Bonus'] += 0.02
normalized_df.loc[selected_df['EPS Growth'] > 0, 'Bonus'] += 0.02
normalized_df.loc[selected_df['PT Upside (%)'] > 15, 'Bonus'] += 0.02

normalized_df['Score'] += normalized_df['Bonus']
  1. we are going to split the dataset into two columns, stability and growth.

stability_weights = {
    'Market Cap': 0.15,
    'Gross Margin': 0.10,
    'Oper. Margin': 0.10,
    'ROIC': 0.10,
    'EPS Growth': 0.10,
    'Return 1Y': 0.10,
    'Top Rating Score': 0.15,
    'Top Analysts': 0.10,
    'Debt-to-Cash': 0.10
}

growth_weights = {
    'Rev. Growth': 0.15,
    'Rev. Growth (Q)': 0.15,
    'Rev. Growth 3Y': 0.10,
    'NetInc Growth (Q)': 0.10,
    'PEG Ratio': 0.10,
    'PT Upside (%)': 0.15,
    'EPS Growth': 0.10,
    'Forward PE': 0.05 if 'Forward PE' in normalized_df.columns else 0
}

normalized_df['Stability Score'] = sum(normalized_df[f] * w for f, w in stability_weights.items() if f in normalized_df.columns)
normalized_df['Growth Score'] = sum(normalized_df[f] * w for f, w in growth_weights.items() if f in normalized_df.columns)
  1. Now we will display top 50 list by rank from 1st to the 50th. Code is below.

normalized_df['Rank'] = normalized_df['Score'].rank(ascending=False)
ranked_df = normalized_df.sort_values(by='Score', ascending=False)
ranked_df = ranked_df.merge(stocks_df[['Symbol', 'Stock Price','Company Name', 'Industry']], on='Symbol', how='left')

# Display top 50 with features and scores

item.title: How to use the library shap properly
item.description:
Once you’ve built and successfully executed your models, the next step is to analyze their results and understand what influences their predictions. This is where the SHAP library becomes extremely useful. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) is a powerful tool for model interpretability in data science. It helps you explain the output of machine learning models by quantifying the contribution of each feature to a prediction.

Why SHAP Matters

Purpose: SHAP explains individual predictions by assigning each feature a contribution value. Core Concept: It’s based on Shapley values from cooperative game theory, which fairly distribute the “payout” (in this case, the prediction) among all features. Importance: Many models—such as XGBoost, LightGBM, and neural networks—are complex and often considered “black boxes.” SHAP makes them transparent by answering:

Which features are most influential globally (across all predictions)? Why was a specific prediction made (local explanation)?

Common Use Cases

Visualizing feature importance. Debugging and improving models. Building trust in AI by making predictions explainable.

In short, SHAP bridges the gap between accuracy and interpretability, enabling you to not only build strong models but also understand and communicate their behavior effectively.

  1. We are going to install pip install shap. code below.
pip install shap

  1. Below is a snapshot from a project I worked on for a major transportation company. While I can’t share the full script due to confidentiality, this example provides an overview of how SHAP was implemented after the model was successfully executed.

Coefficients tell you global importance, but for individual predictions, use:

SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations): Shows how each feature pushes prediction toward TERMINATED or ACTIVE. LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations): Explains one prediction by approximating locally.

import shap
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Prepare SHAP values for the pipeline
X_transformed = final_pipeline.named_steps['preprocessor'].transform(X_test)
explainer = shap.Explainer(final_pipeline.named_steps['model'], X_transformed)
shap_values = explainer(X_transformed)

# 2. Get feature names from the preprocessor
feature_names = final_pipeline.named_steps['preprocessor'].get_feature_names_out()

# 3. Convert SHAP values to DataFrame
shap_df = pd.DataFrame(shap_values.values, columns=feature_names)

# 4. Extract original feature names (before one-hot encoding)
# Example: "categorical__Type_Contract" → "Type"
original_features = [name.split('__')[1].split('_')[0] for name in shap_df.columns]
shap_df.columns = original_features

# 5. Aggregate SHAP values by original feature (mean absolute value)
feature_importance = shap_df.abs().mean().groupby(shap_df.columns).sum().sort_values(ascending=False)

#"Ops Mgr", "Fleet Mgr"

exclude_features = [] 
filtered_importance = feature_importance[~feature_importance.index.isin(exclude_features)]


# Plot top 50 after filtering
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
filtered_importance.head(50).plot(kind='bar', color='teal')
plt.title("Top 50 Features by SHAP Importance")
plt.ylabel("Mean Absolute SHAP Value")
plt.xlabel("Feature")
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


# Optional: Save to CSV
feature_importance.to_csv("shap_feature_importance.csv")
print("✅ SHAP feature importance saved to shap_feature_importance.csv")
✅ SHAP feature importance saved to shap_feature_importance.csv

# Exclude features that contain Ops Mgr or Fleet Mgr (case-insensitive)
exclude_keywords = ["Ops Mgr", "Fleet Mgr"]
pattern = '|'.join(exclude_keywords)

coef_df_filtered = coef_df_sorted[~coef_df_sorted['Feature'].str.contains(pattern, case=False)]
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Extract feature names and coefficients from pipeline
feature_names = final_pipeline.named_steps['preprocessor'].get_feature_names_out()
coefficients = final_pipeline.named_steps['model'].coef_[0]

# Create DataFrame
coef_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Feature': feature_names,
    'Coefficient': coefficients
})

# Add absolute value for sorting
coef_df['AbsCoefficient'] = coef_df['Coefficient'].abs()

# Sort by absolute coefficient
coef_df_sorted = coef_df.sort_values(by='AbsCoefficient', ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

# Exclude features containing Ops Mgr or Fleet Mgr
exclude_keywords = ["Ops Mgr", "Fleet Mgr"]
pattern = '|'.join(exclude_keywords)
coef_df_filtered = coef_df_sorted[~coef_df_sorted['Feature'].str.contains(pattern, case=False)]

# Plot top 50 features after filtering
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 10))
plt.barh(coef_df_filtered['Feature'].head(50), coef_df_filtered['Coefficient'].head(50), color='teal')
plt.title("Top 50 Features by Coefficient (Logistic Regression)")
plt.xlabel("Coefficient Value")
plt.ylabel("Feature")
plt.gca().invert_yaxis()  # Largest at top
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Optional: Save to CSV
coef_df_filtered.to_csv("logistic_coefficients_filtered.csv", index=False)
print("✅ Filtered coefficient data saved to logistic_coefficients_filtered.csv")
✅ Filtered coefficient data saved to logistic_coefficients_filtered.csv
